evidence.claim: Switchbacks over Big Walker Mountain, where the interstate takes a tunnel
evidence.quote: Descending via a long series of short switchbacks down the other side of the mountain ridge

evidence.claim: Switchbacks over Big Walker Mountain, where the interstate takes a tunnel
evidence.quote: carries Interstate 77 through and under Big Walker Mountain

evidence.claim: US 52 crosses Walker Mountain at Big Walker Lookout, with a hairpin turn at the ridge and a long series of short switchbacks on the Bland side.
evidence.quote: passing Big Walker Lookout tower at a hairpin turn just at the ridge of the mountains.  Descending via a long series of short switchbacks down the other side of the mountain ridge, there is an interchange with I-77 in the community of Bland.

evidence.claim: The Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway also includes State Route 717, which follows the east fork of Stony Creek through the Seven Sisters area.
evidence.quote: State Route 717, part of the Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway, passes through the area along the east fork of Stony Creek.

evidence.claim: The Wilderness Society recognizes Seven Sisters as a “Mountain Treasure,” worthy of protection from logging and road construction.
evidence.quote: Seven Sisters, a wildland in the George Washington and Jefferson National Forests of western Virginia, has been recognized by the Wilderness Society as a special place worthy of protection from logging and road construction.  The Wilderness Society has designated the area as a "Mountain Treasure".

evidence.claim: A different crossing opened in 1972: the 4,229-foot Big Walker Mountain Tunnel, completed after five years of construction.
evidence.quote: The 4,229-foot (1,289 m) tunnel was first opened in 1972 after five years of construction labor.

evidence.claim: Carrying I-77 beneath the mountain, it cut the journey from Wytheville to Bland County by 30 minutes.
evidence.quote: The opening of the tunnel reduced the travel time from Wytheville to Bland County by 30 minutes.

evidence.claim: The lookout above predates that change: its tower was built in 1947.
evidence.quote: The tower was originally built in 1947

evidence.claim: Start at Bland, the county seat once called Bland Court House.
evidence.quote: Bland is a census-designated place (CDP) in and the county seat of Bland County, Virginia, United States. Bland was originally known as Bland Court House.

evidence.claim: From the Bland side, the switchbacks lead up to the lookout at the ridge; beyond it, US 52 descends toward Wytheville.
evidence.quote: Leaving Wytheville along Stoney Fork Road, US 52 begins its steep climb across the peak of the Blue Ridge Mountains, passing Big Walker Lookout tower at a hairpin turn just at the ridge of the mountains.  Descending via a long series of short switchbacks down the other side of the mountain ridge, there is an interchange with I-77 in the community of Bland.

evidence.claim: The byway’s Route 717 section connects US 52 with Stony Fork Campground, the Seven Sisters trailheads and I-77 at exit 47.
evidence.quote:
Starting from the access at exit 47 on VA 717, points along the way include:

1.1 mile, access to Stony Fork Creek road
1.25 mile, eastern trailhead of Seven Sisters Trail, on left
1.5 mile, Astin homesite, access to Stony Fork Creek
3.8 miles, Stony Fork Campground, Stony Fork Creek, Stony Fork Nature Trail, Seven Sisters Trail
4.3 miles, junction with US 52, turn right

evidence.claim: Bland was originally called Bland Court House and remains the seat of Bland County.
evidence.quote: Bland is a census-designated place (CDP) in and the county seat of Bland County, Virginia, United States. Bland was originally known as Bland Court House.

evidence.claim: At Bland, US 52 meets I-77 after its descent from Big Walker Mountain.
evidence.quote: Descending via a long series of short switchbacks down the other side of the mountain ridge, there is an interchange with I-77 in the community of Bland.

evidence.claim: North of here, US 52 takes the name Scenic Highway and climbs another ridge to meet the Appalachian Trail south of Bastian.
evidence.quote: From here northwards, the road is known as Scenic Highway, and it again crosses another ridge of mountains, steeply climbing to meet the Appalachian Trail south of the community of Bastian.

evidence.claim: Big Walker Lookout adds a 100-foot observation tower to the crest of Big Walker Mountain.
evidence.quote: Big Walker Lookout is a 100 feet (30 m) observation tower located in the Blue Ridge Highlands Region atop Big Walker Mountain

evidence.claim: Built in 1947, the tower has been run continuously by the Kime family.
evidence.quote: The tower was originally built in 1947 and has been run continuously by the Kime family.

evidence.claim: The store beside it is a replacement: the first building burned in 2003, and a new one was built to its right.
evidence.quote: The first store building burned in 2003 and a new store was built just to the right of the first.

evidence.claim: The swinging bridge that once connected the old store to the tower survived the fire.
evidence.quote: Originally, visitors crossed to the tower by way of a swinging bridge that connected to the back of the old general store. The swinging bridge was not destroyed in the fire and still stands.

evidence.claim: From the lookout, the north approach to the interstate tunnel can be seen below.
evidence.quote: The north tunnel approach and surrounding area can be viewed from the Big Walker Lookout

evidence.claim: The swinging bridge survived the fire that destroyed the original store.
evidence.quote: The swinging bridge was not destroyed in the fire and still stands.

evidence.claim: The Seven Sisters Trail follows Little Walker Mountain’s crest, passing along seven knobs.
evidence.quote: the Seven Sisters Trail, a 4.8 mile, yellow-blazed, difficult,  hiking-and-mountain-bike trail that climbs from 2500 feet to 3300 feet while passing along seven knobs.

evidence.claim: The 4.8-mile trail rises from 2,500 to 3,300 feet and is rated difficult.
evidence.quote: the Seven Sisters Trail, a 4.8 mile, yellow-blazed, difficult,  hiking-and-mountain-bike trail that climbs from 2500 feet to 3300 feet

evidence.claim: Its crest offers views of Griffith Knob, the Big Bend of Walker Mountain and the Stony Fork Valley.
evidence.quote: The Seven sisters Trail, following the crest of Little Walker Mountain, offers  good views of nearby Griffith Knob, the Big Bend of Walker Mountain and the Stony Fork Valley.

evidence.claim: Below the ridges, the wildland contains the upper East Fork Stony Fork watershed, between Walker Mountain and Little Walker Mountain.
evidence.quote: The area includes the watershed of upper East Fork Stony Fork between Walker Mountain on the north and Little Walker Mountain on the south.

evidence.claim: State Route 717 passes through along the east fork of Stony Creek.
evidence.quote: State Route 717, part of the Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway, passes through the area along the east fork of Stony Creek.

evidence.claim: At $50 million, the tunnel was then the most expensive single project on Virginia’s Interstate system. Singstad & Kehart of New York designed the roadway and tunnel after preliminary studies by Richmond engineers Brokenborough & Watkins.
evidence.quote: It carried a price tag of $50 million (equivalent to $284 million in 2024), which at the time was the most expensive single project undertaken on Virginia's Interstate system.

evidence.claim: Singstad & Kehart of New York designed the roadway and tunnel after preliminary studies by Richmond engineers Brokenborough & Watkins.
evidence.quote: Preliminary engineering studies for the project were made by Brokenborough & Watkins, consulting engineers of Richmond, Virginia, and the final design of the roadway and tunnel was by Singstad & Kehart, consulting engineers of New York City.

evidence.claim: The lookout’s site is at an elevation of 3,405 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: Located at an elevation of 3,405 feet (1,038 m)

evidence.claim: The Seven Sisters Trail follows Little Walker Mountain’s crest, passing along seven knobs.
evidence.quote: The Seven sisters Trail, following the crest of Little Walker Mountain

evidence.claim: The surrounding ridges run northeast to southwest, with sandstone and shale above parallel valleys eroded from limestone or shale.
evidence.quote: Ridges, composed of sandstone and shale, run northeast–southwest, with parallel valleys created from limestone or shale.

flags: The cache names the Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway but does not document its Virginia designation date, designation rationale, or the full catalog corridor including SR 617. Those claims are omitted.
Drive runs from Bland toward the lookout and Seven Sisters, following the strip-map order; the cache itinerary describes the reverse direction.
Bland is shorter than the usual moment range because the relevant evidence is thin. The current draft’s “about three hundred” population is dropped; the cache gives 383 in 2020.
US 52 source calls the crossing Blue Ridge Mountains; other cache pages place it in the Ridge and Valley province. Use the named mountain rather than repeat the conflicting regional label.
No site-manager source verifies current tower admission or trail access; no access promise is made.
